name: ToolNet: Connecting Large Language Models with Massive Tools via Tool Graph
venue: arXiv:2403.00839 [cs.AI; cs.CL] (preprint, submitted 29 Feb 2024, v1). Not a peer-reviewed venue; an OpenReview submission PDF exists (openreview.net/pdf/b978cbbfe6c59f7fcb3631e0313b3254f3ef860e.pdf) but no accepted-venue record was found.
authors_affiliation: Xukun Liu (Northwestern University), Zhiyuan Peng (North Carolina State University), Xiaoyuan Yi (Microsoft Research Asia), Xing Xie (Microsoft Research Asia), Lirong Xiang (NC State University), Yuchen Liu (NC State University), Dongkuan Xu (NC State University). Lead author: Xukun Liu; senior/corresponding: Dongkuan Xu (NC State). Collaboration between NC State, Northwestern, and Microsoft Research Asia.
code_url: N/A: no official code repository was located. The arXiv page and the lead author's publication page (https://xukunliu.com/publication/2024-toolnet) list no code link; arXiv provides TeX source only. [uncertain]
maintained_repo_url: N/A (no maintained leaderboard/paper-list repo for this work; it is indexed in third-party survey lists such as github.com/quchangle1/LLM-Tool-Survey and github.com/AngxiaoYue/awesome-llm-tool-learning).
task_domain: tool-use (LLM tool/API learning at scale): selecting and chaining the correct tool/API from a massive library (up to ~3992 APIs) to solve multi-hop tasks; evaluated on tool-augmented QA (science QA, table math, math) and large-scale multi-task tool-calling.
problem_setting: Interactive, single-agent, in-context (training-free) tool use. At each step the LLM (gpt-3.5-turbo) takes the current observation o_s and a bounded interaction history C_s (a queue of size K of past observation-thought-action tuples), produces a thought t_s, then emits an action a_s = (tool, args), receives a new observation from the environment, and iterates up to a maximum of 8 steps until an Answer/Finish tool is called. The central problem is that prompting all tools as a plain-text list does not scale to thousands of tools: token consumption explodes and the LLM hallucinates/mis-selects as |T| grows. ToolNet is a plug-and-play framework (no LLM finetuning) that, instead of exposing the full tool set T at every step, exposes only a small successor subset T_s = pi(T, a_{s-1}) defined by a weighted directed tool graph G under a Markov (last-tool) assumption. Supervision: no model training; the graph is built from tool-use trajectories (static, 2-gram-style transition counts) and/or refined online by an LLM tool Evaluator that scores each used tool in [-3,3], whose accumulated scores reweight edges. The setting includes adversarial/noisy tools (deliberately broken tools) and sudden tool failures to test robustness.
what_is_retrieved: tools (the candidate set of next tool/API nodes). At step t=0 a semantic similarity retriever (or ToolBench's fine-tuned BERT tool retriever) retrieves the K most relevant starting tools from the full library; at every subsequent step the 'retrieval' is graph traversal returning the out-neighbor successor tools of the previously used tool, each annotated with a transition weight. Tool descriptions (and weights) are the retrieved content injected into the prompt.
retrieval_grounding: HYBRID. The retrievable store is the tool graph G over a (largely static) external tool/API library, but the edge weights form a GROWING/episodic structure: in dynamic construction an LLM Evaluator's per-tool scores accumulate over iterations and continuously update transition weights online, so the structure the agent navigates evolves with experience (down-weighting broken/noisy tools, raising backup tools). The tool nodes themselves come from a static API corpus (ToolBench/APIBank etc.); the graph edges are an agent-written, online-updated overlay.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Variable, neighborhood-constrained selection rather than a fixed global top-k over all tools. At t=0 a fixed-K top-K retrieval seeds the starting tool(s) (K=8 for ToolBench baselines, K=5 for APIBank; ToolNet/ToT use only the single most-recommended starting tool). Thereafter each step exposes the (small) set of graph successors (typically <6 by the sparsity analysis) and the LLM picks one. The implicit objective is to recover the correct multi-hop tool SEQUENCE (task completion / win rate), not a single global ranking; per-step candidate sets are precision-driven and small.
retrieval_unit: tool-API (one tool/API = one graph node). The retrievable/injected unit is a tool node together with its transition-weight-annotated successor set (out-neighbors). At t=0 the unit is a single tool's description (semantic-retrieval candidate). There is no document/snippet/trajectory unit; the unit is the tool node and its outgoing edges.
index_source: Hybrid: tool nodes come from a static external tool corpus (ToolBench 3451/3992 APIs, APIBank tools, or 16 hand-set tools for the task-specific QA datasets). The GRAPH (edges/weights) is built two ways: (1) static / offline-induced from existing completed tool-use trajectories via 2-gram transition counting (Eq. 5), available for ToolBench/APIBank/ToolAlpaca-style data; and (2) dynamic / online/test-time-induced, initialized either from static counts or as a fully-connected uninformative graph and then updated each iteration by an LLM Evaluator's tool scores (Eqs. 6-7). The task-specific QA experiments use purely dynamic construction (no public trajectories), starting from a fully-connected equal-weight graph.
index_structure_topology: Dependency/transition GRAPH: a weighted directed graph G=(V,E) with V = T plus special 'start' and 'end' nodes. Each tool is a node; a directed edge (v_i, v_j, w_{i,j}) encodes the transition preference from tool i to tool j (estimated from trajectory transition statistics, i.e. P(next=v_j | cur=v_i)). 'start' connects to all tools (the t=0 candidate pool), every non-special node has a self-loop, and all nodes can transition to 'end'/Finish. Sparsity is the design goal (most tools have <6 successors), so each node's out-neighborhood is the small candidate set surfaced to the LLM. This is a flat (non-hierarchical) tool-transition graph, distinct from category->tool hierarchies or bipartite dependency KGs.
retriever_type: Hybrid / two-stage: (a) the next-tool selection at each step is effectively LLM-as-retriever constrained by the graph — the graph deterministically yields the successor candidate set and the LLM picks among them (the 'retriever' is the graph traversal policy pi plus the LLM); (b) the t=0 starting-tool retrieval uses dense semantic similarity search (tool-description embeddings ranked vs the task-description embedding) or, on ToolBench, the provided fine-tuned BERT Tool Retriever. No BM25 reported.
retriever_learning_signal: LM-feedback / interactive experience (not contrastive or RL-policy training). The traversal 'retriever' (the graph) is learned in two ways: (1) static construction is unsupervised frequency estimation — transition weights = empirical 2-gram transition probabilities from completed trajectories (Eq. 5), no learning of a model; (2) dynamic construction uses LM feedback: an LLM Evaluator scores each used tool as a discrete integer in [-3,3] based on whether the final answer was correct and which tools were helpful/noisy/erroneous; accumulated scores s_i^{(n)} are mapped by f(x) and normalized into edge-weight gradients (Eqs. 6-7) that interpolate (via beta) with the static prior. The t=0 semantic retriever / ToolBench BERT retriever is off-the-shelf (BERT fine-tuned in ToolBench, not by this paper). No gradient training of the underlying LLM.
query_construction: Two query types: (1) t=0 starting-tool query = the raw initial task/question description o_1, embedded and matched against tool-description embeddings (or fed to the ToolBench BERT retriever). (2) Per-step 'query' is implicit and structural: the previously used tool a_{s-1} indexes its successor set in the graph (Markov assumption), so no semantic query is formed at intermediate steps — the prior tool itself is the key. The LLM's thought t_s and weights are then used to pick among the surfaced successors. No sub-query decomposition or query expansion.
query_granularity: Both task-level and step-level (two-level). Task-level: a single semantic retrieval at t=0 selects the starting tool(s) from the whole library. Step/state-level: at every subsequent step the candidate set is regenerated as the graph successors of the last-used tool (per-step, last-action-conditioned), so candidate selection is interleaved with each action.
when_to_retrieve: Iterative (per-step). Candidate-set generation happens at every reasoning step: t=0 semantic retrieval for the starting tool, then graph-successor lookup at each subsequent step until Finish/end or the max of 8 iterations. Not one-shot; not uncertainty-triggered (retrieval is on a fixed per-step schedule, deterministically driven by the previous action).
retrieval_trigger_signal: Fixed schedule (per-step, deterministic). The next-candidate set is produced every step as a function of the last action (T_s = oneigh(v_{s-1})); there is no learned router, token-confidence, attention/uncertainty, or reflection-token trigger gating WHEN to retrieve. (The separate Evaluator that UPDATES the graph is invoked reflectively after a trajectory completes, but that governs memory writing, not retrieval triggering.)
reranking: Yes, lightweight weight-based ordering: within each step the successor tools are sorted by their transition weights and formatted in that order as input context, so higher-weight tools are presented as 'more recommended'. This is a preference-weighted ordering / soft rerank of the candidate set rather than a cross-encoder or RRF reranker. The ablation (Table 5) shows the numeric format of these weights matters (integer / x10 best).
retrieved_context_refinement: Candidate-set restriction + weight annotation: instead of refining retrieved documents, ToolNet prunes the candidate set to the small successor neighborhood (token reduction) and annotates each candidate with a confidence/transition weight that is sorted into the prompt. The interaction history C_s is also a bounded size-K queue (FIFO) to cap context. No distillation, decompose-recompose, or distractor-filtering of retrieved text content.
tool_document_engineering: Minimal: tool descriptions are used largely as provided by the source datasets (e.g. ToolBench API docstrings), formatted as input text alongside the transition weight. The key engineering is (a) compressing each tool description into a semantic embedding for t=0 retrieval and (b) attaching a numeric transition/confidence score to each surfaced tool, with the score's numeric formatting (integer vs decimal, scaling x10) shown (Table 5) to materially affect performance. No synthetic-query augmentation or instruction-tuned tool embeddings.
index_content_separation: Partial / implicit: only the small successor set's tool descriptions and weights are loaded into the prompt at each step (progressive, neighborhood-by-neighborhood disclosure of the tool library), rather than loading all tools' content. There is no explicit separate lightweight index-vs-heavy-content tier (e.g. SOP-index-then-content); the graph itself acts as the lightweight index that gates which tool descriptions are surfaced. [uncertain] on finer separation details.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Live-updated graph with RapidAPI/RESTful tool backends. The tool graph supports online updates so it adapts to tools being added, updated, or crashing (a tool that breaks at iteration 50 is rapidly down-weighted and a backup revived). The underlying tools are real-world RapidAPI / RESTful APIs (ToolBench, drawn from RapidAPI; APIBank tools), called via function-calling style actions (tool name + JSON arguments). No MCP and no automatic CRUD schema sync are described; updates are to edge weights, not to a live-synchronized tool schema registry.
tool_dependency_awareness: Yes — central. ToolNet explicitly models inter-tool dependency as the weighted directed transition graph: the edge weight w_{i,j} captures how often / how preferably tool j follows tool i (output-of-A-feeds-B style chaining observed in multi-hop trajectories). The motivating analysis (Fig. 2) shows tools have a sparse set of successor tools. This is dependency-as-transition-statistics (Markovian last-tool conditioning), not a typed prerequisite/auth dependency graph, and edge weights are dependency-aware via both 2-gram counts and Evaluator feedback.
how_retrieved_used: Prompt augmentation with candidate restriction + preference signal. At each step the LLM prompt contains the bounded history, the current observation/thought, and only the successor tool subset (tool names/descriptions) sorted by transition weight, with an explicit instruction that 'tools with higher scores are more recommended.' The LLM then chooses one tool to call. The retrieved structure thus both constrains the action space (token-efficient) and injects a learned preference prior to guide selection; it is not used as a training signal for the LLM (no finetuning).
planning_integration: Per-step interleaved retrieve-and-act within a sequential ReAct-style loop, where the retrieval (candidate generation) is the navigation step of a graph walk. The LLM 'plans' implicitly by traversing G: thought -> choose successor tool -> act -> observe -> next successors, up to 8 steps. Reflexion can be layered on top (ToolNet+Reflexion) to add trajectory-level self-reflection. No MCTS/explicit tree search inside ToolNet itself (ToT is a baseline, not the integration); planning is a guided sequential graph walk rather than plan-then-retrieve.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Per-tool-call (per-step): retrieval/candidate-generation is interleaved at the granularity of each tool call / each ReAct step within the rollout (one successor-set lookup and one tool choice per step), not per-CoT-token or per-answer.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not case-based reasoning; no retrieved prior case is adapted). The closest analogue is that accumulated tool-use experience (Evaluator scores) adapts the transition weights, which in turn changes which candidates are surfaced — an execution-feedback-driven adaptation of the retrieval structure, not adaptation of a retrieved solution.
retrieved_item_representation: Surface form injected = tool names/descriptions plus a numeric transition/confidence weight per candidate, sorted by weight, embedded in the ReAct-style prompt (thought-action format). The 'start' candidate set is the K semantically retrieved tool descriptions. No distilled strategy text, executable program, or latent token; the injected representation is structured tool-list-with-scores.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Low abstraction / concrete tool: the retrieved unit is a concrete tool/API (single candidate tool) plus its transition-preference score. The graph encodes a procedural transition prior over tools, but each retrieved item is a raw tool, not a distilled strategy, guideline, reusable workflow, or full trajectory.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Experience-driven down-weighting via the LLM Evaluator: failed/incorrect trajectories cause noisy or broken tools to be scored low (in [-3,3]), reducing their transition weights so they are surfaced less or not at all; backup/redundant tools are correspondingly up-weighted. Demonstrated by (a) deliberately injected noisy tools on the QA datasets whose scores stay ~0 while effective tools rise (Fig. 3), and (b) a tool crashing at iteration 50 being swiftly supplanted by a fallback (Fig. 4). Robustness thus comes from online graph reweighting and tool redundancy, plus the candidate-set restriction that limits exposure to irrelevant tools — not from retriever-aware SFT or a separate relevance evaluator on retrieved docs.
memory_type: graph (a weighted directed tool-transition graph) functioning as procedural/experiential memory. Experience is encoded into edge weights rather than stored as episodic trajectories; the graph is the persistent memory across tasks/iterations.
write_back: true: the LLM Evaluator writes accumulated tool scores back into the graph as updated transition weights (Eqs. 6-7) during dynamic construction, so experience is persisted into the structure. (No raw trajectory or case store is written; the write-back target is the edge weights.)
online_growth: true (for the graph weights/structure): in dynamic construction the graph is updated online at every iteration as new trajectories are generated and scored, allowing it to accommodate new tasks, new tools, and tool failures at test time. The node set (tool library) is largely fixed, but the navigable structure (edges/weights, effectively which successors are reachable/preferred) grows and adapts during deployment.
write_back_trigger: Reflective, after-trajectory (and per-iteration in dynamic construction): once a tool-use trajectory completes, the LLM Evaluator inspects the whole trajectory and scores each used tool conditioned on whether the final answer was valid/incorrect and which tools were helpful or noisy/erroneous; these scores then update the weights. Writes happen on both successful and failed trajectories (success raises helpful tools, failure lowers noisy/broken ones). In static construction, weights are written once offline from completed (successful) trajectories. Not per-step and not human-validated.
failure_experience_usage: Both success and failure are used (contrastive-style reweighting). The Evaluator explicitly assigns higher scores to tools that helped produce a valid final answer and lower (negative, down to -3) scores to noisy, erroneous, or unhelpful tools when the answer is wrong or absent; broken tools are detected and down-weighted. Failure experience is thus stored implicitly as reduced transition weights (corrective signal) rather than as explicit failed-case exemplars.
memory_evolution_update: Delta-update / interpolation: edge weights evolve via w_{i,j}^{(n)} = beta * w_{i,j}^{(0)} + (1-beta) * Delta w_{i,j}^{(n)}, where the prior (static) weight is blended with a normalized gradient derived from accumulated Evaluator scores (f(x): alpha*x+1 for x>=0, e^{alpha*x} for x<0). Scores accumulate across iterations (s_i^{(n)} = sum of Delta_i^{(k)}), so weights are continuously refined/overwritten rather than append-only; alpha controls update speed, beta the prior-vs-learned trade-off. Edges can be effectively pruned by down-weighting.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: Partially. Tool selection is governed by a graph-defined policy pi(T, a_{s-1}) whose edge weights are LEARNED from experience (frequency statistics + LLM-Evaluator-driven weight updates), so the candidate-surfacing/preference is a learned-from-feedback policy rather than fixed cosine top-k. However it is not an RL/value-learned action policy (no soft Q-learning / M-MDP / policy-gradient training); the final tool choice among surfaced candidates is still made by the frozen LLM conditioned on the weights. So: learned retrieval STRUCTURE, heuristic/LM-driven update rule, no RL.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No: single-agent setup with one shared tool graph used by that agent across iterations/tasks. The graph is shared across a task stream (experience carries over between tasks), but there is no multi-agent or cross-framework experience sharing studied. [uncertain] whether the graph would be reused across distinct deployments.
benchmarks: Five datasets (subsets used due to cost): (1) SciQA / ScienceQA (1,000 randomly sampled questions, 16 tools incl. noisy); (2) TabMWP (test1k subset, 16 tools); (3) MATH (level-5 only, geometry excluded, 675 questions, 16 tools); (4) API-Bank (lv1-lv2-samples subset, 212 questions, 49 APIs); (5) ToolBench (random 1,000 questions from the G1 set; reports 3992 APIs available). gpt-3.5-turbo as the LLM; max 8 iterations.
benchmark_family: tool (ToolBench, API-Bank) plus tool-augmented QA / math (ScienceQA, TabMWP, MATH used as tool-use environments with injected noisy tools). Primary family = tool-use benchmarks; the three QA/math sets are repurposed as controlled tool-selection-with-noise testbeds.
baselines: ReAct (Yao et al. 2022), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), and Tree-of-Thought / ToT (Yao et al. 2023). Also ReAct (clean) — ReAct with all deliberately-noisy tools removed — as a reference/upper-bound on the QA datasets. On the multi-task datasets, baselines are augmented with the ToolBench fine-tuned BERT tool retriever (K=8 candidates per step; K=5 for APIBank). A combined ToolNet+Reflexion variant is also reported.
key_metrics: Answer quality + efficiency: Exact Match (EM) on SciQA, TabMWP, MATH, and API-Bank; Win Rate (via ToolBench's built-in ToolEval, powered by gpt-3.5-turbo) on ToolBench (no unique ground truth). Efficiency: number of tokens consumed (input + generated) for task completion, and number of reasoning steps (#Steps).
headline_result: ToolNet matches or beats baselines while using far fewer tokens. On TabMWP and MATH it uses only 16.4% and 22.8% of Reflexion's tokens; on SciQA/TabMWP it improves EM by >=10% absolute over the best competitor (SciQA EM 0.61 vs ReAct 0.45 / Reflexion 0.48; TabMWP EM 0.67 vs ToT 0.57). On the massive-tool sets it is on par with Reflexion in win rate while using only 38.5% (APIBank) and 49.7% (ToolBench) of Reflexion's tokens; ToolNet+Reflexion gives the highest scores (APIBank EM 0.83, ToolBench Win Rate 0.75). The paper headlines up to 2.6x greater token efficiency.
ablations: (1) Noisy-tool robustness: ReAct vs ReAct(clean) shows large degradation when noisy tools are present, while ToolNet's tool scores keep effective tools rising and noisy tools near 0 (Fig. 3). (2) Sudden tool failure (Fig. 4, APIBank GetUserToken): a primary tool crashed at iteration 50 is rapidly down-weighted and a functionally identical fallback tool revived — demonstrating dynamic-construction resilience. (3) Transition-weight format ablation (Table 5, APIBank): removing weights (EM 0.70) or scaling to decimals (/100 EM 0.70, /10 EM 0.71) is worst; integer weights (EM 0.75) and x10 (EM 0.75) are best, with token use also dropping as weights scale up — LLMs are more sensitive to integer/large-number differences than to small decimals; performance saturates at x10. (4) Complementarity: layering Reflexion onto ToolNet further raises win rate / EM.
evaluation_decoupling: No: only end-to-end task metrics (EM, win rate) plus efficiency (tokens, steps) are reported. There are no standalone intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) for the tool retriever or graph navigation; retrieval quality is observed only indirectly via tool-score trajectories (Figs. 3-4) and final task performance.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Mixed, mostly outcome with some process signals. Outcome: EM / win rate. Process/efficiency: number of reasoning steps (#Steps) and tokens per task (a process-efficiency measure), plus qualitative per-tool score trajectories (Figs. 3-4) and a reasoning-process visualization (Appendix B) illustrating step-wise tool selection quality; but no quantified step-wise selection accuracy or trajectory-quality score.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Token efficiency is the headline tradeoff. ToolNet attains comparable/better answer quality with markedly fewer tokens and steps: e.g. TabMWP 4,062 tokens / 3.7 steps vs Reflexion 6,594 / 5.3 and ToT 24,710 / 11.3; MATH 6,602 vs ToT 28,886; APIBank 1,649 tokens vs Reflexion 4,286; ToolBench 6,575 vs Reflexion 13,217 and ToT 10,167. Reported up to 2.6x token efficiency. Cost of the approach: extra LLM Evaluator calls for dynamic construction and the need for multi-hop tool-use trajectories to build the graph (named as a limitation). No wall-clock latency / dollar-cost numbers.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Budget-capped via two mechanisms: (a) the interaction history C_s is a fixed-size-K FIFO queue (oldest tuple popped at capacity); (b) the per-step candidate set is the sparse successor neighborhood (typically <6 successors per the Fig. 2 sparsity analysis), so far fewer than |T| tool descriptions are ever in context. At t=0 the starting-tool count is fixed-K: K=8 for ReAct/Reflexion/ToT on ToolBench, K=5 on APIBank, while ToolNet/ToT receive only the single top-recommended starting tool. Successors are reranked by transition weight before being placed in the prompt.
benchmark_construction_and_size: N/A: ToolNet introduces no new benchmark; it evaluates on subsets of existing datasets (ScienceQA 1,000; TabMWP test1k; MATH level-5 non-geometry, 675; API-Bank lv1-lv2 subset, 212; ToolBench G1, 1,000 of 3992 APIs). Answer verifiability: EM against ground truth for the QA/math/API-Bank sets; LLM-judged win rate (ToolEval) for ToolBench, which has no unique ground-truth answer.
builds_on: ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) as the underlying step-by-step tool-calling loop; Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) for trajectory-level self-reflection (used as baseline and as a complementary add-on); ToolBench/ToolLLM (Qin et al. 2023) for the massive RapidAPI tool corpus, trajectories, BERT tool retriever, and ToolEval; Shao et al. 2023 (prompting LLMs with candidate answer scores) and Shinn et al. 2023 (verbal reflection) motivate the score-annotated prompting and tool-level reflection. Graph weights are a 2-gram language-modeling analogue over tool transitions.
contrasts_with: Methods that prompt LLMs with all tools as a flat plain-text list (ReAct, Chameleon, HuggingGPT) which do not scale and ignore inter-tool dependency; finetuning-to-master-tools approaches (Toolformer, ToolkenGPT, Gorilla, ToolLLM) which are costly and poorly adaptable to new/updated tools; beam-search tool exploration (Xie et al. 2023 self-evaluation) which multiplies token cost and lacks an explicit reusable memory; and naive semantic tool retrieval, argued to be coarse/inaccurate when |T| is large and when the thought t_s is generated without full knowledge of T. Table 1 contrasts #APIs (ToolNet 3992), adaptability, token efficiency, planning style (NL+Graph), and plug-and-play.
lineage: Group E (tool-use), large-scale tool-retrieval/organization sub-lineage. Positioned as a training-free, structure-based alternative to (a) finetuned massive-tool models (Gorilla, ToolLLM/ToolBench, ToolkenGPT) and (b) flat-list in-context tool prompting (ReAct/Chameleon/HuggingGPT). It introduces a tool-transition GRAPH as the index/organization, presaging later graph- and dependency-aware tool-retrieval work; sibling to dependency/graph-structured tool-retrieval methods.
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve: yes (graph-successor candidate retrieval + t=0 semantic retrieval), Reuse: partial (transition-weight preference reused to guide selection, not a prior solution reused), Revise: yes-as-weights (Evaluator-driven online reweighting revises the navigation structure), Retain: yes-as-weights (updated weights persisted in the graph)]. It realizes a retrieve-evaluate-update loop over tool transitions rather than over problem-solution cases.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is framed as graph-based tool organization with reflection-driven weight updates, not CBR.
